blocks.text: The last stages of a large power-plant steam turbine have blades 1 m long, yet the high-pressure end of the same machine has blades only a few centimetres tall. Between them, the engineer must decide how much of each stage's pressure drop is taken in the fixed nozzles and how much in the moving blades. That split, the degree of reaction, sets the blade speed and the losses.

blocks.markdown: An axial turbine **stage** is a row of fixed **nozzles (stator)** followed by a row of moving **rotor blades**. Steam or gas expands, converting enthalpy to kinetic energy, and the rotor extracts it as shaft work. We label the stage inlet 1, the nozzle exit (rotor inlet) 2 and the rotor exit 3. In this lesson we assume a repeating stage: constant axial velocity $c_x$ and $c_1=c_3$, so the stage work equals the static enthalpy drop $h_1-h_3$.

blocks.title: Degree of reaction
blocks.text: The **degree of reaction** $R$ is the fraction of the stage's static enthalpy drop that occurs across the rotor: $R=(h_2-h_3)/(h_1-h_3)$. An **impulse** stage has $R=0$: all expansion occurs in the nozzles, and the relative speed through the rotor is unchanged in magnitude. A **50 per cent reaction** stage has $R=0.5$: nozzle and rotor share the expansion equally, so the rotor triangles are mirror images of the nozzle triangles.

blocks.caption: Stage work per unit mass from the whirl change; reaction from the relative whirl components (constant c_x and U)

blocks.title: Triangles, work and reaction of one stage
blocks.prompt: A repeating axial stage has $c_x=180$ m/s and blade speed $U=250$ m/s. The nozzles discharge at $\alpha_2=60^\circ$ from axial and the flow leaves the rotor with no absolute whirl ($c_{\theta3}=0$). Find the stage work and the degree of reaction.

steps.text: Rotor inlet relative whirl, $w_{\theta2}=c_{\theta2}-U$, and rotor outlet relative whirl, with $c_{\theta3}=0$.
Check using the rotor enthalpy drop $h_2-h_3=(W_3^2-W_2^2)/2$.

blocks.answer: The stage work is about 77.9 kJ/kg and the degree of reaction is about 0.376, so a moderate reaction stage.

rows: Equal at inlet and outlet; no static pressure drop in the rotor
Rises through the rotor; static pressure falls in the rotor
Blade speed for a given work (axial exit)
Little pressure drop over rotor, small leakage and axial thrust
More tip leakage and axial thrust
blocks.caption: Impulse and 50 per cent reaction stages compared (axial exit assumed)

blocks.markdown: **Why this matters.** If the exit whirl is zero, $w=U c_{\theta2}$ and $R=1-c_{\theta2}/(2U)$. Setting $R=0$ gives $c_{\theta2}=2U$, so $w=2U^2$; setting $R=0.5$ gives $c_{\theta2}=U$, so $w=U^2$. For the same work, an impulse stage therefore needs a blade speed lower by a factor $1/\sqrt2$, but this leaves the nozzle jet moving much faster, and **friction and kinetic losses grow roughly with the square of the velocities**. Reaction stages handle smaller jet velocities and tend to reach higher peak efficiency, at the price of more stages.

blocks.title: Impulse versus 50% reaction for the same work
blocks.prompt: Each stage must produce $w=80$ kJ/kg with axial exit and $c_x=150$ m/s. Compare the blade speed and the nozzle exit velocity for an impulse stage and a 50% reaction stage.
blocks.answer: The impulse stage runs at 200 m/s against 283 m/s for the reaction stage, but its nozzle jet is faster (427 m/s against 320 m/s) with about 1.8 times the kinetic energy.

items: Draw the nozzle triangle first: $c_x$ and $\alpha_2$ give $c_{\theta2}$ and $c_2$.
Subtract $U$ from $c_{\theta2}$ to obtain the relative inlet whirl, then apply the rotor outlet angle or the zero-exit-whirl condition.
Stage work is $U\Delta c_\theta$; reaction follows from the relative whirl components.
Check consistency by computing the rotor enthalpy drop $(W_3^2-W_2^2)/2$ against the stage work.

blocks.title: The blade-speed and loss trade-off
blocks.text: For a fixed stage work, 50 per cent reaction requires a higher blade speed, which is limited by centrifugal stress, whereas impulse stages run slower but with faster jets and more nozzle loss. Impulse stages are favoured where a large enthalpy drop must be taken in few stages (the first stage, or small turbines); reaction stages are favoured for efficiency in long multi-stage expansions.

points: A stage has a nozzle row and a rotor row; stage work is $w=U(c_{\theta2}-c_{\theta3})$.
Degree of reaction $R=(h_2-h_3)/(h_1-h_3)$; for axial exit $R=1-c_{\theta2}/(2U)$.
Impulse ($R=0$) needs $w=2U^2$ and fast nozzle jets; 50 per cent reaction needs $w=U^2$, higher blade speed, smaller jets and usually lower loss.

questions.stem: The degree of reaction of an axial turbine stage is defined as:

options.text: the static enthalpy drop across the rotor divided by the static enthalpy drop across the whole stage
the static enthalpy drop across the nozzles divided by the drop across the whole stage
the work output divided by the stagnation enthalpy at inlet
the blade speed divided by the nozzle exit velocity

questions.correctOptionText: the static enthalpy drop across the rotor divided by the static enthalpy drop across the whole stage

distractorRationale.a: Correct: rotor drop over stage drop.
distractorRationale.b: This is the complement, $1-R$, the fraction taken in the nozzles.
distractorRationale.c: This is a stage efficiency-like ratio, not the reaction.
distractorRationale.d: This is a velocity ratio and is not the degree of reaction, though it is related through the velocity triangles.

questions.explanation: Degree of reaction measures how much of the expansion occurs in the moving blades: $R=(h_2-h_3)/(h_1-h_3)$. A value of zero means all expansion is in the nozzles (impulse), and 0.5 means an equal split.

questions.stem: Which statement about an impulse stage ($R=0$) is correct?

options.text: All of the static enthalpy drop occurs in the rotor, and the nozzles only turn the flow
There is no static enthalpy drop across the rotor, so the magnitude of the relative velocity is unchanged through the blades
The rotor relative velocity at outlet is much larger than at inlet
The stage produces no work because there is no pressure drop across the rotor

questions.correctOptionText: There is no static enthalpy drop across the rotor, so the magnitude of the relative velocity is unchanged through the blades

distractorRationale.a: Reverses the roles: in an impulse stage the nozzles do all the expansion.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: no enthalpy drop in the rotor means equal relative speed at inlet and outlet.
distractorRationale.c: That is a feature of reaction stages where relative speed increases through the rotor.
distractorRationale.d: Work comes from the whirl change; an impulse stage produces substantial work by turning the high-speed jet.

questions.explanation: In an impulse rotor the relative speed is constant (neglecting friction) since $h_2-h_3=(W_3^2-W_2^2)/2=0$. The work arises from turning the relative flow, which changes the whirl.

questions.stem: An axial turbine stage has blade speed 300 m/s, a whirl velocity of 420 m/s at rotor inlet and $-150$ m/s at rotor outlet (negative meaning against the rotation). The stage work per unit mass is:

distractorRationale.a: Adds the signed whirls instead of subtracting, so it underestimates the change in whirl.
distractorRationale.b: Ignores the outlet whirl, which only holds if the flow leaves axially.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: blade speed multiplied by the full whirl change of 570 m/s.
distractorRationale.d: Uses a kinetic-energy difference, not the Euler work.

questions.explanation: The whirl change is $420-(-150)=570$ m/s, so $w=U\Delta c_\theta=300\times570=171\,000$ J/kg. The reversed outlet whirl adds to the work rather than subtracting from it.

questions.stem: Two stages with axial exit produce the same work per unit mass: one is impulse and the other 50 per cent reaction. The blade speed of the impulse stage compared with the reaction stage is:

options.text: higher, by a factor of about 1.41
the same, because the work is the same
lower, by a factor of about 0.71 ($1/\sqrt2$)

questions.correctOptionText: lower, by a factor of about 0.71 ($1/\sqrt2$)

distractorRationale.a: Reverses the relation: the impulse stage extracts $2U^2$, so it needs less blade speed.
distractorRationale.b: The work per $U^2$ differs, so the blade speeds differ.
distractorRationale.c: Applies a ratio of two to the blade speed, forgetting that work scales with $U^2$.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the ratio of blade speeds is the square root of one half.

questions.explanation: With axial exit, $w=2U^2$ for impulse and $w=U^2$ for 50 per cent reaction, so $U_{imp}/U_{reac}=\sqrt{1/2}=0.707$. The impulse stage turns the flow harder, so it needs less blade speed for the same output.

questions.stem: In a turbine stage, the static enthalpy drop across the nozzles is 42 kJ/kg and across the rotor is 18 kJ/kg. The degree of reaction is:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the rotor drop is 18 out of the 60 kJ/kg total.
distractorRationale.b: Divides the rotor drop by the nozzle drop instead of the total drop.
distractorRationale.c: This is the nozzle fraction, the complement of the reaction.
distractorRationale.d: Assumes an equal split without using the data.

questions.explanation: The stage drop is $42+18=60$ kJ/kg and the rotor takes 18 of it, so $R=18/60=0.30$. Always divide by the total stage drop, not by the nozzle drop alone.

questions.stem: A repeating turbine stage with axial exit has blade speed 220 m/s and nozzle exit whirl 330 m/s. Using $R=1-c_{\theta2}/(2U)$, find the degree of reaction.
questions.explanation: $R=1-330/(2\times220)=1-0.75=0.25$. This is a lightly reacting stage, between impulse (0) and 50 per cent reaction (0.5).

questions.stem: A turbine stage has $c_x=160$ m/s and blade speed $U=260$ m/s. The nozzles discharge at 62° from axial. The relative flow leaves the rotor at 50° from axial against the rotation (so the relative whirl at exit is $-c_x\tan50^\circ$). Find the stage work in kJ/kg.
questions.explanation: Nozzle whirl $c_{\theta2}=160\tan62^\circ=300.9$ m/s. Outlet relative whirl is $-160\tan50^\circ=-190.7$ m/s, so $c_{\theta3}=U+w_{\theta3}=69.32$ m/s. Work is $U(c_{\theta2}-c_{\theta3})=260\times231.6=60215$ J/kg.

questions.stem: An impulse stage with axial exit must produce 60.0 kJ/kg. Using $w=2U^2$ for this case, find the required blade speed in m/s.
questions.explanation: Setting $2U^2=60\,000$ gives $U=\sqrt{30\,000}=173.2$ m/s. A 50 per cent reaction stage for the same work would need $\sqrt{60\,000}=244.9$ m/s, about 1.41 times higher.

questions.stem: Compare an impulse stage with a 50 per cent reaction stage for the same work per unit mass with axial exit. Discuss blade speed, nozzle exit velocity, the sources of loss and the number of stages needed for a given total enthalpy drop.
markingGuide: Impulse: w = 2U^2 so U = sqrt(w/2); 50% reaction: w = U^2 so U = sqrt(w); the impulse stage needs lower blade speed by 1/sqrt(2)
At lower blade speed the nozzle exit velocity (c_theta2 = 2U) is larger for impulse, so higher nozzle kinetic energy and friction losses
Reaction stage: smaller jet velocity, symmetric blading with accelerating relative flow, which tends to give higher peak efficiency
Reaction stage has pressure drop over the rotor so more tip leakage and axial thrust, whereas impulse stage has little
Impulse stage handles larger enthalpy drop per stage at a given blade speed (psi = 2 vs 1), so fewer stages; reaction needs more stages or higher blade speed
Concludes with typical use: impulse for first stage or small turbines, reaction for efficient multi-stage expansion
questions.explanation: The key relation is stage work per $U^2$: impulse gives 2 and 50 per cent reaction gives 1 (axial exit). The impulse stage therefore passes more work through slower blades but needs a faster jet, with higher kinetic-energy loss, while the reaction stage trades a higher blade speed or more stages for lower velocities and better efficiency.

questions.stem: Explain how the degree of reaction of a stage can be calculated from velocity triangles when the exit flow is axial. Derive $R=1-c_{\theta2}/(2U)$, stating the assumptions, and state what value of $c_{\theta2}/U$ corresponds to impulse and to 50 per cent reaction.
markingGuide: Assumptions: constant axial velocity, repeating stage (c1 = c3), constant blade speed U
Stage work w = U c_theta2 (axial exit, c_theta3 = 0) equals h1 - h3
Rotor enthalpy drop h2 - h3 = (W3^2 - W2^2)/2 and W^2 = c_x^2 + w_theta^2
With w_theta3 = -U and w_theta2 = c_theta2 - U, h2 - h3 = (U^2 - (c_theta2 - U)^2)/2 = c_theta2 (2U - c_theta2)/2
Impulse: c_theta2 = 2U; 50 percent reaction: c_theta2 = U
questions.explanation: The rotor enthalpy drop comes from the change of relative kinetic energy, and the stage drop equals the work $Uc_{\theta2}$. Their ratio simplifies to $1-c_{\theta2}/(2U)$, which is zero when $c_{\theta2}=2U$ and one half when $c_{\theta2}=U$.
